introduction-the-trust-problem.core: BGP was designed in 1989 for a small community of trusted operators. Routers accept announcements from neighbours without proof that the origin AS is authorised to announce the prefix, or that the path is real. One misconfiguration or malicious actor can redirect traffic worldwide. BGP security layers cryptographic attestations (RPKI) and validation onto that trust-based system.

first_principles.problem: In 2008 a national ISP's attempt to block YouTube locally leaked a more-specific route and took YouTube offline globally.
truths: Authorisation can be published and checked.

analogy.title: A town where anyone can put up road signs
analogy.story: Most residents are honest, but one prankster can divert all traffic.
analogy.breaks: Fake signs are local; BGP mistakes are global.

example.title: 2008 incident
flow: ISP announces YouTube /24 internally to block it

check.q: What fundamental check does classic BGP lack?
check.a: Verification that the announcing AS is authorised to originate the prefix (and that the path is real).

bgp-hijacks-stealing-the-traffic.core: Hijack types include exact-prefix origin hijacks (competing with the real route), more-specific hijacks (always winning by longest match), and path manipulation (forged AS_PATH that keeps the real origin to evade simple checks). Motives range from accidents to theft: in 2018 attackers hijacked Amazon Route 53 prefixes to steal cryptocurrency via fake DNS answers.

first_principles.problem: Attackers hijack a DNS provider's prefixes for two hours and redirect a crypto wallet site to a phishing server.
truths: Origin checks alone miss forged paths.
DNS and TLS can amplify hijack impact.
derivation: Use **DNSSEC and TLS** to limit hijack impact.

analogy.title: Mail redirection fraud
analogy.story: A fraudster files a change of address for your street (more-specific) and all your post goes to them.
analogy.breaks: Postal fraud needs paperwork; BGP hijacks need just a router.

example.title: 2018 Route 53 hijack
flow: Users accepting bad TLS cert lose funds

check.q: Why can't RPKI origin validation alone stop a forged-path hijack?
check.a: The attacker keeps the legitimate origin ASN at the end of the AS_PATH, so the origin check passes.

route-leaks-the-middleman-mistake.core: A route leak happens when an AS propagates routes beyond their intended scope, typically when a customer re-announces routes learned from one provider or peer to another provider. The leaker becomes an unintended transit network, overwhelming its links and adding huge latency. Leaks are usually accidental (missing export filters), and prevention means strict customer filters, max-prefix limits and RFC 9234 roles with Only-To-Customer (OTC).

first_principles.problem: In 2019 a small ISP's optimiser leaked thousands of more-specific routes through Verizon, disrupting Cloudflare and others.
truths: Providers often accept too much from customers.
derivation: Export to providers **only your and customer routes**.

analogy.title: A neighbour letting through-traffic cut across their garden
analogy.story: They didn't mean to become a road, but now everyone drives through and the lawn is destroyed.
analogy.breaks: Gardens are visible; leaks are only noticed by monitoring.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only own/customer routes leave; role checks catch leaks.

code.text:
route-map TO-UPSTREAM permit 10
 match community OWN-OR-CUSTOMER
route-map TO-UPSTREAM deny 100
!
router bgp 64500
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 local-role customer
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 maximum-prefix 50

check.q: What makes a route leak different from a hijack?
check.a: A leak propagates legitimate routes beyond their intended scope; a hijack announces routes the AS isn't authorised to originate.

rpki-the-passport-system.core: RPKI is a public key infrastructure for internet number resources. RIRs issue resource certificates to address holders, who use them to sign objects (ROAs) stating which ASNs may originate their prefixes. Relying-party validators (Routinator, rpki-client, Fort) fetch and verify all objects from the RIR repositories and feed validated payloads to routers via the RTR protocol.

first_principles.problem: Routers have no authoritative way to know which AS is allowed to announce a prefix.
truths: RIRs know who holds which addresses.
Routers need a compact, validated feed.

analogy.title: A passport system for IP addresses
analogy.story: The government (RIR) issues passports (certificates); holders issue signed authorisations, and border guards (validators) check them.
analogy.breaks: Passports are carried; RPKI objects are fetched from repositories and can be stale if fetches fail.

example.title: Run a validator

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Routers query validator via RTR for VRPs.

code.text:
routinator init --accept-arin-rpa
routinator server --rtr 0.0.0.0:3323 --http 0.0.0.0:8323 &
curl -s localhost:8323/api/v1/validity/AS13335/1.1.1.0/24 | jq .validated_route.validity.state
# "valid"

example.outcome: cryptographic origin data available to routers.

check.q: What do routers receive from an RPKI validator?
check.a: Validated ROA Payloads (prefix, maxLength, origin ASN) via the RTR protocol, used to judge route origins.

roa-the-authorization-letter.core: A Route Origin Authorization states: 'prefix P, up to maxLength M, may be originated by AS X.' The address holder creates it in the RIR portal or via delegated RPKI. Set maxLength to exactly what you announce: a loose maxLength (/24 for a /22 you announce as /22) lets attackers announce forged-origin more-specifics that still validate. Multiple ROAs cover multiple origins, such as a DDoS-scrubbing provider.

first_principles.problem: A ROA with maxLength /24 for an announced /22 lets an attacker forge-origin a /24 that RPKI marks valid.
truths: ROAs define allowed origins and lengths.
Loose maxLength widens the attack surface.

analogy.title: A signed letter authorising a specific agent
analogy.story: 'Alex may collect parcels for flat 12, but not for the whole building.'
analogy.breaks: Letters are checked by one clerk; ROAs are checked by thousands of routers.

code.text:
prefix 198.51.100.0/22  maxLength 22  origin AS64500   # normal announcement
prefix 198.51.100.0/24  maxLength 24  origin AS64500   # announced during DDoS
prefix 198.51.100.0/24  maxLength 24  origin AS19551   # scrubbing provider
prefix 192.0.2.0/24     maxLength 24  origin AS0       # unused space: never valid

check.q: What does an AS0 ROA mean?
check.a: No AS is authorised to originate the prefix, so any announcement of it is invalid (protects unused space).

route-validation-states.core: Route origin validation compares each received route to the VRPs. Valid: a VRP covers the prefix with a matching origin and allowed length. Invalid: covering VRPs exist but the origin or length doesn't match. NotFound: no VRP covers the prefix. The recommended policy is to drop Invalid and accept Valid and NotFound, since much of the internet still lacks ROAs. Major networks now drop Invalids.

first_principles.problem: A network enables ROV but sets 'prefer Valid' instead of 'drop Invalid', so hijacked routes still propagate via other paths.
derivation: Monitor **invalid counts** and your own status.

analogy.title: A guest list at the door
analogy.story: On the list with matching ID: in. On the list with the wrong ID: out. Not on any list: allowed in for now.
analogy.breaks: Doormen can make exceptions; routers apply policy uniformly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Invalid routes never enter the table.

code.text:
rpki
 rpki cache 10.0.0.53 3323 preference 1
!
route-map RPKI-IN deny 10
 match rpki invalid
route-map RPKI-IN permit 20
!
router bgp 64500
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 route-map RPKI-IN in

check.a: Many legitimate prefixes still lack ROAs; rejecting NotFound would break reachability to a large part of the internet.

bgp-flowspec-the-global-firewall.core: BGP Flowspec (RFC 8955) distributes traffic-filtering rules through BGP: match on destination and source prefix, protocol, ports, packet length or TCP flags, then rate-limit, drop, mark or redirect. During a DDoS, an operator can push a precise rule ('drop UDP from port 123 to 203.0.113.45') to every edge router in seconds, much more surgical than blackholing the whole IP.

first_principles.problem: RTBH stops a DDoS by blackholing the victim IP, completing the attacker's goal of taking it offline.
truths: BGP already reaches every edge router.

analogy.title: A city-wide alert to police checkpoints
analogy.story: 'Stop only red vans heading to the stadium' rather than closing every road to the stadium.
analogy.breaks: Police judge context; a bad flowspec rule can drop legitimate traffic everywhere at once.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Attack dropped at every edge; the service stays online.

check.q: What advantage does Flowspec have over RTBH?
check.a: It filters only attack traffic matching specific criteria, keeping the victim reachable, whereas RTBH drops all traffic to the IP.
